items.readable_text:
Content:
How do we solve an equation with a variable raised to an even exponent, such as

Content:
[MATH: x^6 = 64?]

Content:
We can solve this equation by taking the [MATH: 6]th root of each side and solving for [MATH: x.]

Content:
Since the exponent [MATH: (6)] is even, there will be two real solutions (positive and negative):

Content:
[MATH: x^{6}|= 64; root(x^{6}, 6)|= ± root(64, 6); x|= ± root(2^{6}, 6); x|= ± 2]

Content:
Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=\pm 2.]

Content:
In general, we have the following rule of thumb:

Content:
> When [MATH: n] is even, and we take the [MATH: n]th root of both sides of [MATH: x^n = a] with [MATH: a \geq 0,] we get two solutions (positive and negative): [MATH: x = \pm\sqrt[n]{a}]

Content:
Watch out! If [MATH: a<0] and [MATH: n] is even, equation [MATH: x^n = a] has no solution since, in this case, [MATH: x^n \geq 0] for any real [MATH: x.]

sections.normalized_html: Find all of the real solutions to the equation [MATH: 9x^4 = \dfrac{1}{9}.]
sections.readable_text: Find all of the real solutions to the equation [MATH: 9x^4 = \dfrac{1}{9}.]

sections.normalized_html:
We can solve this equation by isolating the [MATH: x^4] term and then taking the [MATH: 4]th root of each side.

First, let's isolate the [MATH: x^4] term on the left-hand side:

[MATH: 9x^{4}|= (1)/(9); x^{4}|= (1)/(81)]

Now, we take the [MATH: 4]th root of each side and solve for [MATH: x.] Since the exponent [MATH: (4)] is even, we consider both the positive and negative solutions:

[MATH: x^{4}|= (1)/(81); root(x^{4}, 4)|= ± root((1)/(81), 4); x|= ± root(((1)/(3))^{4}, 4); x|= ± (1)/(3)]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=\pm \dfrac13.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
How do we solve an equation with a variable raised to an even exponent, such as

Content:
[MATH: x^6 = 64?]

Content:
We can solve this equation by taking the [MATH: 6]th root of each side and solving for [MATH: x.]

Content:
Since the exponent [MATH: (6)] is even, there will be two real solutions (positive and negative):

Content:
[MATH: x^{6}|= 64; root(x^{6}, 6)|= ± root(64, 6); x|= ± root(2^{6}, 6); x|= ± 2]

Content:
Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=\pm 2.]

Content:
In general, we have the following rule of thumb:

Content:
> When [MATH: n] is even, and we take the [MATH: n]th root of both sides of [MATH: x^n = a] with [MATH: a \geq 0,] we get two solutions (positive and negative): [MATH: x = \pm\sqrt[n]{a}]

Content:
Watch out! If [MATH: a<0] and [MATH: n] is even, equation [MATH: x^n = a] has no solution since, in this case, [MATH: x^n \geq 0] for any real [MATH: x.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Solving Equations With Even Exponents

Example Prompt:
Find all of the real solutions to the equation [MATH: 9x^4 = \dfrac{1}{9}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can solve this equation by isolating the [MATH: x^4] term and then taking the [MATH: 4]th root of each side.

First, let's isolate the [MATH: x^4] term on the left-hand side:

[MATH: 9x^{4}|= (1)/(9); x^{4}|= (1)/(81)]

Now, we take the [MATH: 4]th root of each side and solve for [MATH: x.] Since the exponent [MATH: (4)] is even, we consider both the positive and negative solutions:

[MATH: x^{4}|= (1)/(81); root(x^{4}, 4)|= ± root((1)/(81), 4); x|= ± root(((1)/(3))^{4}, 4); x|= ± (1)/(3)]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=\pm \dfrac13.]
